beneficiaries_note: The location the sheet's bottom line reads (row labels naming Nigeria).

missing_data.note: Thin: the children treated for acute malnutrition are counted, but no trial measures the treatment against none: the deaths it averts rest on case series of untreated wasting and a judged share averted, as in our own builds.

summary: Treats children with acute malnutrition in Gombe State, Nigeria. The Happier Lives Institute's estimate of the life-improving wellbeing effects of Taimaka's treatment (WELLBYs per $1,000), rebuilt from the figures in its report.

source.title: Does a well-fed infancy make for a more felicitous life? How treating malnutrition impacts happiness: a charity evaluation of Taimaka

resources.title: HLI, How treating malnutrition impacts happiness: a charity evaluation of Taimaka (2024)
resources.note: HLI publishes no public spreadsheet for this estimate: the model is built from the inputs and figures stated in the report's text, each quoted on its row. HLI links GiveWell's CMAM model and Taimaka's own cost sheet, not a sheet of its own.

resources.title: HLI, 2025 giving season charities update
resources.note: Rates Taimaka a Promising Charity and restates the figure as 68 WELLBYs per $1,000 (5.43 WELLBYs at $87 a child, which works out at 62); the report's 65.6 is what this model reproduces.

sections.title: HLI's estimates by source of evidence (report Table 5)
sections.explainer: HLI has no randomised trial of treating acute malnutrition with wellbeing outcomes, so it extrapolates from three other bodies of evidence and averages them with equal weight. Each estimate below is HLI's, after its adjustments for validity, generalisability and charity-level factors.

sections.title: Lives saved and grief averted
sections.explainer: charityevals' step, from HLI's own appendix. HLI's bottom line counts only the life-improving effects; it puts the lives saved (65 WELLBYs per $1,000 for someone who holds that death deprives a person of the happy years they would have had, with a neutral point of 2) and grief averted (2.88) aside as a bonus that depends on philosophical views. The site counts the lives every model saves, each valued with the weight on a life under Your values, so here the wellbeing of the years saved is scaled by it, as in HLI's model of the Against Malaria Foundation. The evaluator view keeps HLI's bottom line, which counts neither.

sections.title: Discounting
sections.explainer: charityevals' step, not HLI's. HLI counts a year of better wellbeing the same whenever it comes. In our view, later years count less at the discount rate under Your values, as in GiveWell's models; the evaluator view sets the rate to 0, so HLI's figure is unchanged there.

sections.title: Staff pay below market
sections.explainer: charityevals' step, not the evaluator's: with credit by share of resources on, staff's pay below what they could earn elsewhere counts as an in-kind contribution and gets its share of the outcome. Off by default.

rows.label: WELLBYs per $1,000: atole protein supplement trial
rows.explainer: From one trial of atole, a protein supplement given to children in Guatemala, followed into adulthood (n = 1,249): 56.84 WELLBYs of direct effect, with HLI's validity (0.26), generalisability (0.41) and charity-level (0.88) adjustments, gives 5.23 WELLBYs per child treated in HLI's table, at $87 a child. (The product of the rounded factors shown is 5.33; HLI's table and its 60.0 are used here.)

rows.label: WELLBYs per $1,000: natural experiments on famine
rows.explainer: From two natural experiments on the long-run scarring of famine (n = 34,724): 11.37 WELLBYs of direct effect, times 0.75, 0.75 and 0.88, is 5.63 WELLBYs per child at $87.

rows.label: WELLBYs per $1,000: small-quantity nutrient supplements (IQ pathway)
rows.explainer: From a meta-analysis of 13 trials of small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (n = 23,588), through their effect on IQ: 17.29 WELLBYs, times 0.43, 0.98 and 0.88, is 6.31 WELLBYs per child at $87. HLI also works out a social-emotional pathway (22.2 per $1,000) but gives it no weight, taking the higher pathway as a floor.

rows.label: WELLBYs per $1,000 (life-improving effects)
rows.explainer: HLI weighs the three sources equally: "we estimate that the life-improving WELLBYs per $1k (WBp1k) generated by Taimaka to be 65.6" (section 5). HLI counts only life-improving effects in this figure; it estimates the lives saved could add about 65 WELLBYs per $1,000 for those who value saving lives highly, and grief averted 3 more, but treats both as bonus effects that depend on unsettled philosophical choices. GiveWell's model of Taimaka (on this site) values the lives saved.

rows.label: HLI's estimate for lives saved, per $1,000 (WELLBYs; deprivationism, neutral point 2)

source.title: HLI report
source.quote: The result of combining these estimates is 65 WBp1k assuming deprivationism and a neutral point of two.

rows.explainer: HLI's average of two estimates, 56 (Taimaka's data in GiveWell's analysis, adapted to wellbeing) and 76 (Taimaka's own analysis), after HLI's counterfactual adjustment.

rows.label: Life expectancy used (Nigeria)

source.title: HLI report
source.quote: Using our estimate of Nigeria's life expectancy (62 years)

rows.label: Average life satisfaction in Nigeria (0–10)

source.title: HLI report
source.quote: for an average of 5.72 on a 0 to 10 scale

rows.label: WELLBYs per life saved, at HLI's neutral point (HLI)
rows.explainer: HLI: a life saved gives 62 × (5.72 − 2) = 231 WELLBYs. Used only to turn HLI's 65 WELLBYs per $1,000 back into lives saved.

rows.label: Lives saved per $1,000, after HLI's counterfactual adjustment
rows.explainer: HLI's WELLBYs from lives saved over its WELLBYs per life: about 0.28 lives per $1,000.

rows.label: Value of averting a child's death (units of value)
rows.explainer: Taimaka treats children under five for acute malnutrition, so each life saved is an under-five death averted: GiveWell's moral weight, 116.25 doubled-income years, times "A child's life vs doubled-income year" (Your values).

rows.label: Value of the lives saved per $1,000, the site's way (units of value)
rows.explainer: Changed for consistency: the site counts the lives a charity saves in every model, valued one way: GiveWell's moral weight for an under-five death (facts: moral_weights) times "A child's life vs doubled-income year" (Your values), not HLI's WELLBYs of the years lived above a neutral point. HLI's bottom line leaves them out (0 here in the evaluator view), as a bonus for those who value saving lives, which it puts at 65 WELLBYs per $1,000 at a neutral point of 2, plus 2.88 for grief averted. HLI's own figure, 62 years × (5.72 − 2) = 231 WELLBYs from birth, undiscounted, is used above only to turn its 65 WELLBYs per $1,000 back into lives saved. Deaths averted now are not discounted. Grief averted for the family is part of what a death costs and is not added on top, as in GiveWell's models.

rows.label: WELLBYs per $1,000 from the lives saved
rows.explainer: The deaths' value in units of value (above), put into WELLBYs at the WELLBY rate ("1 point more life satisfaction for a year vs doubled-income year", Your values). The unit's conversion multiplies every WELLBY by the same rate, so the two cancel: the deaths count their shared value whatever the WELLBY slider says, and only the WELLBYs HLI measured move with it. The one row a model may read the WELLBY rate in (docs/normalization.md 2.3, INV-17).

rows.label: Discount rate on future wellbeing
rows.explainer: The shared discount rate (Your values). HLI doesn't discount, so the evaluator view pins it at 0.

rows.label: Years the wellbeing effect lasts, from treatment

source.title: HLI report
source.quote: a wellbeing effect of approximately between 0.09 to 0.46 standard deviations (SDs) per person that lasts 62 years

rows.explainer: HLI's duration for the effect of treatment in early childhood: to about age 62.

rows.label: Years from treatment until the benefit is counted, on average
rows.explainer: Our judgment from HLI's own timing: in the atole and famine estimates the harm grows linearly until age 25 and is constant after; in the SQ-LNS (IQ) estimate the benefit runs from age 16 to 62. A single start 12 years after treatment (it matches the discounting of HLI's profiles at 4%), with the WELLBYs spread evenly from then to the end, stands in for these profiles; 0 is HLI's undiscounted view, 16 the IQ pathway's.

rows.label: Discount factor for the timing of the benefit
rows.formula: (1 + discount_rate_per_year) ^ -effect_start_years * pv_annuity_due(1, discount_rate_per_year, effect_duration_years - effect_start_years) / (effect_duration_years - effect_start_years)
rows.explainer: The WELLBYs spread evenly from the start year to the end of the effect, discounted to today, as a share of their undiscounted total: 1 at a 0% rate.

rows.label: WELLBYs per dollar, discounted
rows.explainer: HLI's life-improving WELLBYs, discounted for when they come, plus the lives saved (not discounted: a death averted now is valued as a whole, as in every model).

rows.label: Staff pay as a share of program cost
rows.explainer: Default for programs where staff deliver the help themselves (treatment, counselling, coaching, outreach): staff pay is about half the cost. Our judgment; we haven't seen this program's breakdown.

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable jobs elsewhere
rows.explainer: Health workers and field staff at nonprofits often earn somewhat less than in comparable jobs. Our judgment.

rows.label: Salary forgone by staff per dollar of cost (in-kind donation)
Share of the full cost paid in cash
rows.explainer: With credit by share of resources, staff's forgone pay counts as part of the cost, and staff get their share of the outcome. Off, this is 100%.

rows.label: WELLBYs per dollar
rows.explainer: The figure per dollar above; with credit by share of resources, times the share of the full cost paid in cash (staff's forgone pay is the rest).
